storylines.label: Routing Inference
storylines.latest_title: How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI

prior_narrative.tldr: This is a loose topical cluster, not one event: three unrelated items that each use "routing" to cut inference cost or latency at a different layer. OpenRouter rebuilt provider routing in its hosted gateway on Oct 30, and a Show HN on Nov 7 introduced Sibyl, an immutable local inference appliance with routing built in.
prior_narrative.whats_new: The arXiv paper C²-Routing (Nov 10) moves routing to the input layer, pairing image cropping with compression as a model-agnostic way to shrink what a vision-language model must process for visual question answering.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: "Routing" now names three separate cost and latency levers (which provider serves a request, which local backend runs it, and how much input reaches the model), and each one is tuned and evaluated differently.

beats.headline: OpenRouter rebuilds provider routing for better, faster inference
beats.summary: Routing at the hosted-gateway layer: choosing which provider serves a request.

beats.headline: Sibyl packages a local inference stack as an immutable appliance with routing
beats.summary: A solo side project, described by its author as early days, that puts routing in a portable self-hosted box configured through a UI.

beats.headline: C²-Routing applies routing to VLM inputs: cropping plus compression
beats.summary: A paper on model-agnostic input reduction for visual question answering, unrelated to either product above.

open_questions: Does OpenRouter publish latency or success-rate numbers that quantify the rebuilt provider routing?
Does Sibyl's routing select among local models and backends only, or can it also fall back to hosted providers?
How much accuracy does C²-Routing give up for its input reduction, and does the result hold across VLMs beyond those the paper tests?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Treat these as three independent decisions. If you send traffic through OpenRouter, re-measure latency and provider distribution after the routing rebuild; evaluate the appliance and the paper on their own evidence before adopting either.

storylines.latest_title: Einsia AI Launches Visual Cipher Bench to Evaluate Long-Horizon Visual Reasoning in AI Agents

prior_narrative.tldr: This is a loose cluster of arXiv papers that share policy- and preference-optimization vocabulary, not one developing story. It spans three research strands: RL recipes for agents (TSBPO, learned multi-agent orchestration, negative-only rewards), preference-optimization variants (DNO, steerable GRPO, PORT, VEPO), and agents that tune GPU kernels and AI infrastructure (Infrathon, AscendGYM).
prior_narrative.whats_new: Nov 16: ViRA applied cross-input relative policy optimization to train visual agents that zoom into ultra-high-resolution images and answer from the evidence rather than common sense.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: RL fine-tuning is being pointed at agent behaviors builders care about (credit over long trajectories, orchestration, tool-gated routing, kernel tuning), but every result here is author-reported on the papers' own benchmarks, not production evidence.

beats.headline: RL recipes target the hard parts of training agents: delayed credit, orchestration and partial verifiers
beats.summary: TSBPO, few-step flow RL, CRESiST for speech translation, learned multi-agent orchestration, and negative-only policy optimization.

beats.headline: Preference-optimization papers target general preferences, shifting objectives, noisy labels and visual grounding
beats.summary: DNO empirical study, steerable multi-objective GRPO with LoRA adapters, PORT token reweighting, and VEPO.

beats.headline: Agents that tune GPU kernels and AI infrastructure get methods and benchmarks
beats.summary: Question-driven kernel agents, a local 7B CUDA study, Infrathon, and the Ascend NPU benchmark AscendGYM.

beats.headline: Optimization moves into serving cost and product decisions
beats.summary: Small-model routing that switches on reasoning, retrieval or tools only when needed, and Airbnb-style cold-start cover-photo selection.

beats.headline: ViRA trains high-resolution visual agents to read evidence instead of guessing

open_questions: Does any independent group reproduce TSBPO's gains on long-horizon agent tasks outside the paper's own environments?
Does negative-only policy optimization train useful agents when the verifier can only reject wrong answers in real tool-use settings?
Do kernel-optimization agents beat vendor libraries and hand-tuned kernels on Infrathon or AscendGYM workloads under their cost accounting?
Can a locally hosted 7B code model produce correct CUDA kernels reliably enough to use without a larger model in the loop?
Does PORT's token-level reweighting hold its advantage when preference-label noise is measured on real production feedback?
Does small-model routing cut compute without a measurable quality drop on traffic other than the study's benchmark?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If you trial an agent for kernel or infra tuning, gate every change on a correctness check before measuring speed and compare against your vendor-library baseline; treat the RL and preference-optimization recipes as candidates for your own eval, not drop-in replacements for DPO or GRPO.

storylines.latest_title: Murmur: Efficient Long-Context ASR Inference with Hierarchical Chunking

prior_narrative.tldr: This is a loose cluster of inference-efficiency work, not one event; reclustering dropped most of the earlier diffusion-LM papers. It opened Oct 30 with pruning, MoE quantization and prompt compression, and by Nov 8-12 added block-diffusion drafters and overlapping block denoising.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Microsoft Research's TokenEconomizer (Nov 17) has AI coding agents learn from past runs to spend fewer tokens, a day after Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B, a 4GB open small model tuned for fast conversational agents.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: The efficiency work is moving from model internals (pruning, MoE quantization, diffusion decoding) to the agent layer, where token spend per task and small on-device models set the bill.

beats.headline: Pruning, MoE quantization and input compression shrink inference cost
beats.summary: Four papers cut cost on the model or input side: extreme-sparsity pruning, Matryoshka MoE with mixed precision, RL-trained prompt compression, and VLM image cropping.

beats.headline: Block-diffusion work targets draft-tree verification and block-boundary latency
beats.summary: The two remaining diffusion-LM papers: D3Tree prunes block-diffusion draft trees for speculative decoding, and overlapping block denoising cuts latency in block diffusion LMs.

beats.headline: Agent papers attack prompt-carried skill memory and wasted delegation
beats.summary: MDSKILL distills skill memory into weights instead of prompts; a deep-research paper argues delegation only pays off when allocation and execution are coordinated.

beats.headline: Efficiency reaches vendors and agent products: Baseten, Nemotron Bolt, TokenEconomizer
beats.summary: The latest items are a serving-vendor post, a small open model for agents, and a lab blog on coding-agent token spend, not arXiv method papers.

open_questions: How much does TokenEconomizer cut tokens per resolved coding task, and on which agent harness and benchmark?
Does Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B hold tool-calling accuracy at 4GB against Gemma-4-E4B-it, the model it was post-trained from?
Does a block-diffusion drafter with a pruned draft tree beat existing drafters on end-to-end throughput under concurrent serving load?
Does any inference framework or vendor ship diffusion LLM serving with parallel decoding?
Do the pruning and MoE quantization gains hold on agentic and long-context tasks, not only perplexity and short benchmarks?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Log tokens per completed agent task before adopting any of these methods, so TokenEconomizer-style savings or a small-model swap can be measured against your own baseline; do not plan capacity around diffusion LLMs yet.

prior_narrative.tldr: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash posted AMD MI355X AgentPerf results by Oct 14, and OrcaRouter priced it against rival models on Oct 16. The Flash-1017 update followed Oct 17-19 with stronger coding, cheaper inference and a public search API, and an independent risk paper appeared Oct 26.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Rival.io launched GraphX on Oct 29, claiming to run DeepSeek V4 Flash on just eight NVIDIA L4 GPUs, a self-hosting cost claim the coverage does not yet back with benchmarks.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Flash is now cheaper per task, has an independent safety evaluation, and has a vendor claiming a small-GPU serving footprint. Hosting cost and risk posture can both be weighed, though the footprint claim is unverified.

status.detail: Flash-1017 is out; a safety paper and a low-GPU serving claim are the newest evidence.

OrcaRouter prices Flash against Nemotron 3.5 and Step 5 Preview
Flash-1017 ships with stronger coding, cheaper inference and a search API

beats.headline: Roundup places Flash-1017 among open releases; a third-party paper evaluates its safety risks
Rival.io's GraphX claims Flash serving on eight L4 GPUs

open_questions: Do independent evals confirm Flash-1017's agentic gains over larger rivals?
Is the new search API priced and rate-limited for production use?
Is the unannounced snapshot a separate model or the same Flash-1017?
What do the paper's loss-of-control and manipulation findings say about Flash-1017 under agentic use?
Does GraphX publish throughput and latency numbers for Flash on eight L4 GPUs?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Rerun your agent eval and cost-per-task numbers on Flash-1017 before switching, read the Oct 26 risk evaluation before granting tool access, and wait for GraphX throughput data before sizing any L4 deployment.

storylines.label: Control Plane
storylines.latest_title: QuadGate – 4-gate control plane that keeps agent KV prefix caches warm SHow HN

prior_narrative.tldr: This is a loose cluster around a shared label, not one developing event. Late October brought two Show HN agent tools calling themselves control planes, flightdeck for observability and Omneum for local context management, and on Nov 4 the vLLM blog introduced Kinference, an open source inference control plane for vLLM on Kubernetes.
prior_narrative.whats_new: GitSeed, posted to Hacker News on Nov 15, applies the label to coding agents: a self-hosted control plane for running AI coding agents.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: "Control plane" now names three different layers: agent observability, coding-agent orchestration, and multi-tenant inference serving. Check which layer a tool actually governs before adopting it.

beats.headline: Two Show HN projects pitch control planes for AI agents
beats.summary: flightdeck targets observability and control of running agents; Omneum targets local, text-blind context management.

beats.headline: Kinference brings an open source control plane to vLLM on Kubernetes
beats.summary: Token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, and load balancing for self-run inference platforms.

beats.headline: GitSeed pitches a self-hosted control plane for coding agents
beats.summary: The label returns to open source agent tooling, scoped to AI coding agents.

open_questions: Does Kinference see adoption or contributions beyond its launch post on the vLLM blog?
Do flightdeck or Omneum gain users or contributors after their Show HN posts?
What does GitSeed actually control for coding agents: sandboxes, permissions, repo access, or just job scheduling?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If you run vLLM on Kubernetes, evaluate Kinference for per-tenant rate limits and cost tracking in a staging cluster. Treat GitSeed, flightdeck and Omneum as early experiments until they show releases and outside contributors.

storylines.label: MoE Inference
storylines.latest_title: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

prior_narrative.tldr: An Oct 27 arXiv paper framed edge MoE inference as an expert-weight movement problem rather than a compute problem. Two Hacker News posts followed within a week, showing the same memory constraint being attacked on a single DGX Spark and on Macs.
prior_narrative.whats_new: A Show HN project (Nov 3) claims faster MoE inference on a Mac with less RAM, following a Nov 2 post on running a 124B MoE on one DGX Spark.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: MoE models only fit small hardware if expert weights are moved or compressed cleverly, so memory footprint, not FLOPs, decides which models you can serve locally.

status.detail: Research and hobbyist projects converge on memory-bound MoE inference on small hardware.

beats.headline: CRISP: pruning plus scheduling for edge MoE
beats.summary: Names expert-weight movement, not compute, as the edge bottleneck.

beats.headline: 124B MoE tuned on a single DGX Spark
Show HN: faster MoE on Mac with less RAM

open_questions: Do the Mac and DGX Spark projects publish tokens-per-second and RAM figures that others can reproduce?
Do practitioner projects adopt expert pruning or scheduling ideas like CRISP's?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If you plan local MoE serving, benchmark peak memory and expert-load traffic on your target hardware before trusting parameter-count estimates.
